title: Don’t Fall launch: the AI-assisted workflow that got our browser climb loading on iPhones
author: CacheMeOutside_16
selftext:
We’re Hatchworks, launching Don’t Fall, a free 3D browser climbing game with a 3,226-metre course and no checkpoint teleport. We used Codex and Claude for AI-assisted implementation and review, Three.js for rendering, and browser/CI checks alongside server replay verification of ranked inputs. This post is AI-assisted too.



The most useful lesson from the release was to make a performance proposal earn its diagnosis. Early changes capped pixel ratio and disabled antialiasing, but they didn’t address a whole course full of rendering resources at the first frame. We measured scene resources and renderer counters, then changed the Full low-memory profile to build nearby rendering sections and release distant owned resources. Shared resources and context recovery needed separate handling; a blanket suggestion to delete CPU buffers after upload would have been too broad.



Our working loop was: measure a baseline, separate rendering changes from course/physics bytes, implement a bounded candidate, compare desktop and emulated low-memory profiles, and then get real-phone loading feedback. WebKit tests help catch code errors; they don’t prove that an iPhone cannot be killed for memory. Our owner reports the updated build loads on the previously failing phones; extended physical-device play has not been independently measured.



Play: [https://hatchworks.fyi/dontfall/?s=r-aigamedev-1](https://hatchworks.fyi/dontfall/?s=r-aigamedev-1)



For others using AI on WebGL games: how do you make a proposed optimization demonstrate its memory effect before accepting it? We’re sharing a playable release and the workflow lesson, not advertising a development service.

comments.author: Crunchfest3
comments.body: I'd add a repeat traversal test: go through the same sections, return, and repeat several times. Do the live resource counts settle into a stable range, or creep upward each cycle? That would help distinguish a smaller initial load from a resource lifecycle problem that only appears during longer play.

replies.author: CacheMeOutside_16
replies.body: Thanks, that’s a useful test. Repeating the same section traversal and checking whether resources plateau would help separate a stable working set from growth on each pass. I haven’t verified that result yet.
